sections.title: Rh Factor and Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn

blocks.x: Humans have 46 chromosomes arranged as 22 pairs of autosomes plus one pair of sex chromosomes: 46,XX in females and 46,XY in males. Each parent contributes 23 chromosomes to the zygote (23 from the egg, 23 from the sperm), so the diploid number of 46 is restored at fertilization. Because the egg always carries an X, and the sperm carries either an X or a Y, it is the father's sperm that determines the sex of the offspring — the Y-bearing sperm produces a son, the X-bearing sperm a daughter. This is sometimes tested as a "which statements are correct" item: normal karyotype = 46 chromosomes, 23 from each parent, males XY/females XX, and sex is fixed by which sperm (X- or Y-bearing) fertilizes the egg — all of these are simultaneously true.
The SRY Gene and Testis Determination

The key trigger for male development is SRY (Sex-determining Region of the Y chromosome), located near the tip of the short arm (Yp) adjacent to the pseudoautosomal region. SRY encodes a transcription factor (an HMG-box DNA-binding protein) that is expressed in the genital ridge and switches on SOX9, which in turn drives differentiation of the bipotential gonad into a testis. Testes then secrete testosterone (masculinizing the Wolffian ducts) and anti-Müllerian hormone/AMH (suppressing the Müllerian ducts). In the absence of SRY/SOX9 signaling, the default pathway is ovarian development. SRY and SOX9 are therefore both classified as mammalian testis-determining genes; a functional X-linked or autosomal gene alone (without SRY signaling) is not sufficient for testis/gonadal development — SRY is the essential trigger.
When SRY Is Misplaced: Sex-Reversal Syndromes
Because SRY sits so close to the pseudoautosomal boundary, an aberrant X–Y recombination event during paternal meiosis can translocate SRY onto an X chromosome, or leave a Y chromosome without it:

items: XX male syndrome (de la Chapelle syndrome): a 46,XX individual with a Y-to-X translocated SRY gene develops as a phenotypic male (testes present) despite lacking most of the Y chromosome. Such individuals are typically infertile because they lack the rest of the spermatogenesis genes carried on the Y (e.g., the AZF regions).

XY female (Swyer syndrome) / gonadal dysgenesis: a 46,XY individual whose Y chromosome lacks a functional SRY (deletion or mutation) fails to form testes; the gonads remain as streak gonads, and external genitalia develop along the female pathway. Mutations further downstream, such as in SOX9 (also causing campomelic dysplasia) or the androgen receptor gene (androgen insensitivity syndrome), can likewise produce a female or ambiguous phenotype in a 46,XY individual even when SRY itself is intact, because the signaling cascade downstream of SRY is disrupted.

blocks.x: X-Inactivation (Lyon Hypothesis) and Barr Bodies

Because females have two X chromosomes but males only one, cells need a dosage compensation mechanism so that X-linked gene products are produced at similar levels in both sexes. Mary Lyon proposed that in every somatic cell of a female, one X chromosome is randomly and permanently inactivated early in embryogenesis (the Lyon hypothesis). The inactivated X becomes highly condensed heterochromatin visible under the microscope as a Barr body (in interphase nuclei) or a "drumstick" appendage on the nucleus of neutrophils. The rule of thumb: the number of Barr bodies = number of X chromosomes − 1. So a normal 46,XX female has 1 Barr body; a 47,XXY (Klinefelter) male has 1 Barr body (chromatin-positive, not negative); a 45,X (Turner) female has 0 Barr bodies (like a normal male); and someone with extra X chromosomes (e.g., 48,XXXX) would have 3.

X-inactivation is not complete, however: genes located in the pseudoautosomal regions — the small segments at the tips of the X and Y that pair during male meiosis — escape inactivation, because these genes need to be expressed from both X copies just as autosomal genes are (they exist in two functional copies in both sexes). This explains why dosage compensation is said to apply to "all X-linked genes except those near the pairing (pseudoautosomal) segments."

X-inactivation is normally random (roughly 50:50 mosaic of cells expressing the maternal vs paternal X), which is why heterozygous carrier females for an X-linked recessive disease are usually asymptomatic — on average half their cells express the normal allele. However, skewed (non-random) X-inactivation can occur by chance or due to selection against cells expressing a deleterious allele, so that a carrier female ends up with a majority of cells expressing the mutant X. Such women can show mild or intermediate symptoms of an X-linked recessive disease (a "manifesting carrier"), for example mild bleeding tendencies in hemophilia carriers or patchy pigmentation in X-linked ocular albinism/incontinentia pigmenti carriers (whose mottled skin patterns directly reflect the mosaic pattern of X-inactivation).

"Sex-linked" traits are those whose genes lie on the sex chromosomes (overwhelmingly the X, since it carries far more genes than the small, gene-poor Y). Sex-linked traits — in contrast to most autosomal traits — are generally recessive in their classic examples, which is precisely why they show a distinctive pattern: much more common in males (who are hemizygous, having only one X) than in females (who need two copies to be affected).
X-Linked Recessive

items: Hemophilia A and B (deficiency of clotting factor VIII or IX respectively) and red-green color blindness are the textbook X-linked recessive traits. Affected males (XᵃY) pass the disease allele to all daughters (obligate carriers) and no sons. A carrier female (XᴬXᵃ) passes the allele to half her sons (who are affected) and half her daughters (who become carriers).

Classic pedigree question: a woman whose father was a hemophiliac must herself be an obligate carrier (she received her father's only X, which carries the mutant allele). If she is expecting a son, that son has a 50% chance of inheriting the mutant X and being a hemophiliac (and a 50% chance of being unaffected); the fact that the fetus is a boy doesn't change the 50:50 odds — it just rules out the "carrier daughter" outcome.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is also X-linked recessive (dystrophin gene) and is therefore rare/uncommon in females (who would need two mutant alleles, or skewed inactivation, or an X-autosome translocation disrupting the normal allele, to be affected) — it is essentially a disease of males. DMD and the milder allelic disorder Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD) are caused by different mutations in the same dystrophin gene (DMD = frameshift/nonsense mutations producing no functional protein; BMD = in-frame deletions producing a partially functional, shortened protein) — so the two conditions are correctly described as allelic to one another.

blocks.x: X-Linked Dominant and Codominant

items: X-linked dominant disorders (e.g., X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets, some forms of Rett-related conditions) are, perhaps counterintuitively, more frequent in females than males, simply because females have two X chromosomes and thus two chances to inherit the dominant allele, while males have only one X.

The Xg blood group is a real example of an X-linked trait, but note it is recessive, not dominant, and its gene lies near the tip of the short arm of the X (in the pseudoautosomal region), not the long arm — these are commonly tested "which statement is wrong" details.

An example of X-linked co-dominant inheritance cited in genetics exams is Becker muscular dystrophy, where heterozygous carrier females can show detectable (intermediate) biochemical or clinical signs rather than being completely silent carriers.

blocks.x: Y-Linked (Holandric) Inheritance

Y-linked traits are passed only from father to son (never to daughters, and never skip a generation) because only males have a Y chromosome. Presence of a beard and other secondary sexual hair patterns in males is cited as an example of a Y-linked/holandric character in classic genetics questions. By contrast, curly hair, leucoderma (vitiligo), and achondroplasia are not sex-linked — they are autosomal traits, a common trap in true/false exam items.
Sex-Limited and Sex-Influenced Genes

Do not confuse "sex-linked" (gene physically located on a sex chromosome) with sex-limited genes, which can be carried on either autosomes or sex chromosomes but are phenotypically expressed in only one sex (e.g., milk yield genes expressed only in females, or beard growth influenced by autosomal genes that require a male hormonal environment to manifest). Note: sex-limited genes are not necessarily located on sex chromosomes — many are autosomal but hormonally restricted in expression.
These arise mainly from nondisjunction — failure of chromosomes to separate properly during meiosis (or occasionally mitosis, producing mosaics) in either parent.

c: Short stature, webbed neck, shield chest, streak (non-functional) ovaries → infertility/amenorrhea, coarctation of the aorta, no Barr body

Classic teaching point: XYY has no obvious effect on sexual phenotype — historically over-associated with behavioral traits, a link now considered largely unsupported

blocks.x: A frequent exam trap: sex-chromosome aneuploidies are actually more common overall than autosomal aneuploidies (most autosomal trisomies other than 21, 18, and 13 are lethal in utero), so "autosomal abnormalities are less common than sex chromosome abnormalities" is the correct statement, not the reverse.

c: Trisomy 21 (47,+21), usually maternal meiotic nondisjunction; risk rises sharply with maternal age

Intellectual disability, characteristic facies, single palmar crease, congenital heart defects; affected males are generally infertile (affected females can occasionally reproduce); average lifespan is reduced compared to the general population, though many now live into adulthood thanks to improved cardiac and medical care — it does not confer a longer-than-average lifespan, and it is not a disorder that "discriminates" by race/ethnicity (it occurs in all populations)
Severe intellectual disability, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, congenital heart defects; most die within the first year

Deletion of short arm of chromosome 5 (5p−)

Deletion of short arm of chromosome 4 (4p−)

blocks.x: Genomic Imprinting: Prader-Willi and Angelman Syndromes

Genomic imprinting is the phenomenon whereby a gene's expression depends on which parent it was inherited from, due to epigenetic marks (chiefly DNA methylation) laid down differently on the maternal and paternal alleles during gametogenesis. The classic teaching example involves reciprocal deletions of the same region, 15q11–q13:

items: Prader-Willi syndrome: deletion of the paternally-derived copy of 15q11–q13 (or maternal uniparental disomy, i.e., inheriting both copies of chromosome 15 from the mother). Features: neonatal hypotonia, hyperphagia and childhood obesity, intellectual disability, short stature, hypogonadism.

Angelman syndrome: deletion of the maternally-derived copy of the same 15q11–q13 region (or paternal uniparental disomy). Features: severe intellectual disability, ataxic "puppet-like" movements, inappropriate happy/laughing demeanor, seizures, absent speech. Angelman syndrome is the textbook "classic example of genomic imprinting."

blocks.x: Note the contrast with Bloom syndrome, an autosomal recessive chromosome-instability disorder (BLM helicase gene defect) associated with sun sensitivity, short stature, and cancer predisposition — sometimes tested because it is one of the few conditions in which a back mutation (reversion) at a somatic level (spontaneous reversion of the mutant allele in some cells) has been documented, producing patches of phenotypically normal ("revertant") skin/tissue.
The ABO system is governed by a single autosomal gene (on chromosome 9) with three main alleles: IA, IB, and i. IA and IB are codominant to each other, and both are dominant to i (recessive).

There are only 4 possible phenotypes (A, B, AB, O) even though there are 6 possible genotypes, because IAIA and IAi are phenotypically indistinguishable (likewise IBIB and IBi). At the molecular level, the A and B alleles encode glycosyltransferase enzymes that differ by only a handful of amino-acid-changing nucleotide substitutions (classically cited as about seven nucleotide differences between the A and B alleles), which is enough to change the enzyme's sugar specificity (adding N-acetylgalactosamine for the A antigen vs. galactose for the B antigen) — a good illustration of how small sequence changes create a big antigenic/phenotypic difference.
Practice Logic for ABO Crosses

items: Father group O (ii) × Mother group AB (IAIB): every child receives an i from the father and either IA or IB from the mother, so children are only group A or group B — 0% chance of group O children, since no child can be ii.
Two group O (ii × ii) parents can only produce group O (ii) children — they cannot have a group A child, since neither parent carries an I<sup>A</sup> allele.

Father group B (I<sup>B</sup>i or I<sup>B</sup>I<sup>B</sup>) × Mother group AB (I<sup>A</sup>I<sup>B</sup>): if the father is heterozygous, children can be A, B, or AB — but never O, since the mother contributes only I<sup>A</sup> or I<sup>B</sup>.

ABO is not influenced by environment — it is a purely genetically determined trait, and this — along with its underlying population genetics (allele frequencies shift via genetic drift, geographic isolation, and selection) — is a commonly tested true/false pairing.

sections.title: Rh Factor and Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn

blocks.x: The Rh system (based mainly on the RhD antigen) is a separate, highly polymorphic blood-group locus from ABO. Individuals are Rh-positive (carry the D antigen) or Rh-negative (do not). Unlike ABO, humans do not naturally have anti-Rh antibodies unless they have been sensitized by prior exposure to Rh-positive blood.

Rh incompatibility / hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN, erythroblastosis fetalis): occurs when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive fetus (having inherited the D antigen from an Rh-positive father). During delivery (or earlier events such as miscarriage, trauma, or amniocentesis), fetal Rh-positive red cells can enter the maternal circulation, sensitizing the mother to produce anti-D IgG antibodies. This first pregnancy is usually unaffected, but in a subsequent Rh-positive pregnancy, maternal anti-D IgG crosses the placenta and destroys fetal red cells, causing anemia, jaundice, and potentially fetal hydrops. This is why Rh-negative mothers are given anti-D immunoglobulin (RhoGAM) prophylactically. Note by contrast that maternal-fetal ABO incompatibility most commonly involves a group O mother carrying an A, B, or AB fetus — because group O individuals naturally have both anti-A and anti-B IgG antibodies (unlike group A or B individuals, whose anti-B or anti-A antibodies are more often IgM, which does not cross the placenta as readily) — though ABO HDN is typically much milder than Rh HDN.

A karyotype (the ordered display of an individual's chromosomes, arrested at metaphase when chromosomes are maximally condensed and each consists of two sister chromatids, making this the ideal stage for counting chromosome number and banding pattern) is used clinically to investigate the cause of recurrent miscarriage, the cause of birth defects in a newborn, and the cause of an individual malignancy (many cancers carry characteristic acquired chromosomal rearrangements) — i.e., all of the above are legitimate indications for karyotyping. In karyotype nomenclature, "p" denotes the short arm, "q" the long arm, "qter" the tip of the long arm, and "mos" or similar notation indicates mosaicism — note that an "i" in this shorthand system denotes an isochromosome, not an inversion (inversions are denoted "inv").
